newsitem.title: RWANDA: Rwandan troops invade east Zaire town - diplomats.
newsitem.headline: Rwandan troops invade east Zaire town - diplomats.

text.p: Rwandan troops entered the eastern Zaire town of Goma on Friday by lake and land to assist Tutsi rebels fighting to capture it, diplomats said.

"There are RPA (Rwandan Patriotic Army) troops in uniforms in the centre of Goma city, the main square. They came in by land and across Lake Kivu on boats landing on the city beach," said a diplomat in the region, quoting witnesses.
"We are 110 percent certain the RPA is in Goma. It is confirmed," added another diplomat, also declining to be identified.
Rwandan Foreign Minister Anastase Gasana denied that Rwandan government troops were involved in fighting in Zaire, but said they were ready to hit back against Zairean shelling.

"If we continue to receive such provocations, such attacks on the part of the Zairean army, we have the right to defend ourselves and to engage in defensive action against the Zairean army if that continues," he told Belgian radio on Friday.
Zaire's ragged army is facing a humiliating defeat against the well-armed rebels in the two eastern provinces of North and South Kivu facing Rwanda and Burundi.
All sides ignored international calls for a ceasefire.
Reuters photographer Corinne Dufka reported on Friday that Bukavu, capital of South Kivu, fell to the Banyamulenge Tutsi rebels on October 30.
Bukavu, about 120 km (75 miles) south of Goma, was the scene of some of the fiercest fighting in eastern Zaire and the Roman Catholic archbishop Christophe Munzihirwa was killed on Tuesday.

Earlier Zairean and Rwandan troops traded fire across the border at Gisenyi, at the north end of Lake Kivu just across the border from Goma, North Kivu's capital and previously the main base for Zaire's army and allied Rwandan Hutu forces.

Inside Goma, aid workers hid under their desks as fighting raged nearby and the United Nations agonised over whether it should pull out its staff and effectively abort its mission to feed 1.1 million Rwandan refugees inside Zaire.

In the past week, Zairean and Rwandan troops have fired at one another across the border at the only two significant Rwandan towns, Gisenyi and Cyangugu, and Rwanda admitted sending troops into Zaire on a military sortie earlier this week.
At Gisenyi on Friday, I saw mortar fire come first from the Zairean side of the border. Thousands of townspeople fled in panic and Rwandan troops began to respond to incoming fire.
The fighting in eastern Zaire has added tens of thousands of displaced people to the hordes of Rwandan and Burundian Hutu refugees moving from camp to camp and fearing the advancing Tutsis.
In Geneva, the U.N. refugee agency UNHCR said before the scale of the battle in Goma was known it had not taken a final decision to evacuate its staff.

The conflict in eastern Zaire pits ethnic Tutsis against both the Zairean government and Hutu refugees, some of whom were responsible for the 1994 genocide in Rwanda of up to one million Tutsis and other victims.
UNHCR chief Sadako Ogata has appealed repeatedly for the refugees to go home.
But Tutsi attacks on the camps have pushed the refugees deeper into Zaire and only about 1,000 Rwandans are reported by the U.N. to have crossed into Rwanda.
Ogata has said she fears a disaster greater than 1994, when some 50,000 newly-arrived Rwandan refugees died of epidemics in stinking, overcrowded camps in eastern Zaire.
Even without an evacuation, U.N. efforts to feed the refugees have been severely hampered by the fighting.
Many of them have been on the run from fighting for at least a week amid fears they will be hit by hunger and epidemics.
The refugees now live in a constant state of panic. "At one point yesterday we had refugees on the road walking in both directions," said Panos Moumtzis, a UNHCR spokesman in Goma.
"They are really panicking. They are very scared. They do not know where to go," he added from his office in Goma city.
In their fight with Kinshasa, the Tutsis accuse the government of President Mobutu Sese Seko, living since August as an invalid in Switzerland, of persecuting them for years.

The Tutsis trace their roots in Zaire back two centuries. They have been refused Zairean citizenship since 1981 and on Friday Zairean state radio reported that parliament voted to purge Tutsis from the army, state companies and public administration. The move must be approved by the government.
A mob of several hundred demonstrators attacked Tutsi-owned property in Zaire's capital Kinshasa on Friday and looted dozens of cars, a Reuters Television cameraman said.
"I saw them smash the windows of two shops said to be owned by Tutsis in central Kinshasa and loot a beer truck. They were driving around in dozens of stolen cars," said Marc Hoogsteyns.
The fighting in east Zaire has already claimed hundreds, perhaps thousands of lives.
In Geneva, Rolin Wavre of the International Committee of the Red Cross, said Zairean Red Cross volunteers in Bukavu had buried at least 100 dead collected from the streets last week.

The conflict in eastern Zaire assumed greater international dimensions with the Kinshasa government adding Uganda to the list of its enemies and more world leaders urging round table peace negotiations.

State Zairean radio on Friday said Zaire's transitional parliament had voted to sever diplomatic relations with Rwanda, Burundi and Uganda, the three neighbours accused by Kinshasa of waging war against the sprawling Central African nation.
